title: US Ends 'Duration of Status' for Student and Journalist Visas — Introduces Four-Year Cap
excerpt: The Trump administration's new rule replaces a 47-year-old policy that allowed F, J and I visa holders to stay indefinitely, creating major implications for over 300,000 Indian students in the US.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • DHS ends the 47-year-old 'duration of status' system for F, J and I visa holders
  • Student and exchange visas now capped at four years; journalist visas at 240 days
  • Grace period after graduation halved from 60 to 30 days
  • Extensions require USCIS approval with biometric checks and fraud screening
  • Current visa holders automatically transition; rule effective 60 days after Federal Register publication
The Trump administration announced Thursday that it is ending the decades-old "duration of status" system for international students, exchange visitors and foreign journalists, replacing it with fixed admission periods that will significantly impact hundreds of thousands of Indian nationals studying and working in the United States. ## What Changes Under the New Rule The new final rule from the Department of Homeland Security establishes a maximum four-year admission period for holders of F visas (students) and J visas (exchange visitors). Foreign journalists on I visas will be limited to stays of up to 240 days, with Chinese journalists facing a shorter 90-day limit. Under the previous system — in place since 1978 — visa holders in these categories could remain in the country for the "duration of status," meaning as long as they maintained valid enrollment or employment. The DHS described this as an arrangement that allowed some to become "forever students" by perpetually enrolling in courses to avoid departure. "For nearly half a century, the outdated 'duration of status' system has compromised national security and created an environment ripe for immigration fraud," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement. ## Impact on Indian Students Indians represent one of the largest international student populations in the United States, with over 300,000 students enrolled across American universities. The new rule means those pursuing programs longer than four years — including many doctoral candidates — will need to apply for extensions through USCIS, subjecting them to biometric verification, background checks and fraud screening. The rule also halves the grace period for F visa holders after completing their studies, reducing it from 60 days to 30 days. This significantly narrows the window available for graduates to leave the country, transfer to another institution or change their immigration status — a period many Indian graduates use to transition to OPT (Optional Practical Training) or prepare H-1B applications. ## Tighter Academic Restrictions Graduate students are now prohibited from changing their "educational objectives" at any point or from transferring to another school without USCIS authorization. This shifts oversight from educational institutions to federal authorities, adding another bureaucratic layer for students navigating an already complex immigration system. Current F, J and I visa holders already in the US will automatically transition to the new framework, with their authorized stay capped at four years from the rule's effective date. ## When It Takes Effect The final rule will be published in the Federal Register in the coming days and take effect 60 days after publication, subject to congressional review. Visa holders who need additional time beyond the four-year cap will be able to apply for extensions, but approval is not guaranteed. The move is part of the Trump administration's broader immigration crackdown that has included increased scrutiny of legal immigration pathways, visa revocations tied to ideological views, and the stripping of legal status from hundreds of thousands of migrants since January 2025. For Indian students and their families, the practical effect is clear: studying in America now comes with a tighter timeline, more paperwork and less certainty about how long they can stay.

author: Diaspora Desk
